la:verb:deruo.html:
dē-rŭo, rŭi, 3, v. a. and n. (a very rare word).
Act., to throw or cast down.
Lit.: hiems immensam vim aquarum ruptis nubibus deruat,.—
Trop., to take away, detract: cumulum de laudibus alicujus, * .—
Neutr., to fall down: Ap. M. 2, p. 128; 7, p. 196.

la:verb:derelinquo.gloss: to forsake, abandon, discard or desert
senses: to forsake, abandon, discard or desert
la:verb:derelinquo.html:
dē-rĕlinquo, līqui, lictum, 3, v. a.
In the class. lang., to forsake wholly, to abandon, desert (good prose): cf.: Ti. Gracchum a Q. Tuberone derelictum videbamus,: ut aratores agros latos ac fertiles desererent totasque arationes derelinquerent,: serere aliquid in inculto et derelicto solo,: naves ab aestu derelictae, * : castra,; cf. 37, 8, 5; 10, 17, 5: in arce praesidium dereliquit,: perditi atque ab omni non modo fortuna, verum etiam spe derelicti,; cf.: ut me quasi pro derelicta sis habiturus,; : communem causam (with deserere),: desertarum derelictarumque rerum patrocinium suscipere,: Dominum, et saep.—
To leave behind: in qua (arce) praesidium dereliquit,: filium quem privatum dereliquerat,; .—
In late Lat., to leave behind, to bequeath: libros de gente Romana conscriptos,: derelictum magnum aes alienum,.

la:verb:deripio.gloss: to tear or snatch off or away; pull or tear down
senses: to tear or snatch off or away; pull or tear down
la:verb:deripio.html:
dē-rĭpĭo (-rupio), rĭpŭi, reptum, 3, v. a.
rapio
,
to tear off, tear away, snatch away, remove violently; to pull down (class., esp. freq. in poets).
Lit. constr., with abl. with or without a prep., or rarely with dat.: aliquem de ara,; so with de, ; ; ; with ab, : vestem a pectore,: ferrum a latere,; with ex: velamina ex humeris,; cf.: aurum matronis,: pellem leoni,: pignus lacertis,; : amphoram horreo,: qualos fumosis tectis,: lunam caelo, et saep.: ensem vaginā,: ramos arbore,: tunicam,: derepta acus,: arma templis,: ore frena,: plaustro derepta nurus,; ; et saep.—Absol.: facinus indignum, erum meum hic luci derupier in via,.—Prov.: e caelo deripit ille deos, of outrageous impiety,.—
Trop.: quantum de mea auctoritate deripuisset,.!*? In MSS. and edd. often confounded with diripio q. v.

la:verb:derigesco.html:
dē-rĭgesco, gŭi, 3,
v. inch. n. (occurring only in the perf.), to become stiff or rigid; to curdle (a poet. word): formidine sanguis deriguit,: deriguere oculi,were fixed,; so, oculi,: hirsutae comae,: manus,: cervix,: Niobe malis, (al. diriguit).

la:noun:derivatio.html:
dērīvātĭo, ōnis, f.
derivo
,
a leading off, turning off, turning away.
Lit.: derivationes fluminum, * : sollemnis (sc. lacus Albani), (cf. shortly before, priusquam ex lacu Albano aqua emissa foret).—
Trop.
In gen.: dictum aliquod in aliquem usum tuum opportuna derivatione convertere,.—
Esp.
In grammat. lang., derivation, etymology of words, Plin. ap. ; ; P. et saep.—
In rhetor.
An exchanging of one word for another of like meaning, to soften the expression (as fortis for temerarius, liberalis for prodigus, etc.), .—
As rhet. fig. = παρηγμένον, the development of a preceding statement or conception into a new thought, Jul. Ruf. Schem. Lex. § 14.

la:verb:derideo.gloss: to laugh at, mock, make fun of, deride
senses: to laugh at, mock, make fun of, deride
la:verb:derideo.html:
dē-rīdĕo, si, sum, 2,
v. a., to laugh at, laugh to scorn; to scoff at, deride (class.).
With acc.: omnes istos deridete atque contemnite,; so with contemnere,: te,: derisus a suis consiliariis,: aliquem,; ; ; : aliquid,; ; : sabbata, et saep.—Prov.: albis dentibus aliquem deridere; v. albus.—
Absol.: Ap. Age dic. Ep. At deridebitis, : derides, in conversation,you mock me, are making game of me,; ; : derisum,: deridet, cum sibi ipsum jubet satis dare Habonium,he is mocking,: Patronus despiciat, derideat,; cf. : quibus derisus Philippus,.—P. a.: dērīsus, a, um, absurd, scorned; only sup.: senex derisissimus,.

la:verb:derivo.html:
dē-rīvo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
rivus
,
to lead, turn, or draw off a liquid, from or to a place.
Prop.: de fluvio aquam,: aqua ex flumine derivata, * : flumen,; ; : derivata in domos flumina, 7; 4, 2, 8; cf.: umorem in conliquias,.—
to disperse, distribute: deriventur fontes tui foras,.—
Trop.
In gen. (repeatedly in Cic.): nihil in suam domum inde,, 72: alia ex his fontibus,; cf.: hoc fonte derivata clades,: derivare auimum curaque levare, to divert, * : derivandi criminis causa,: iram alicujus in se,: culpam in aliquem,; cf. : culpam derivare in rem,: partem aliquam curae et cogitationis in Asiam,: exspectationem largitionis agrariae in agrum Campanum,: alio responsionem suam,.—
Esp., in gramm., to derive, sc. one word from another (postAug. for ducere), ; ; P. et saep.

la:verb:derogo.gloss: to take away, diminish, remove, withdraw, (with dative) detract from
senses: to take away, diminish, remove, withdraw, (with dative) detract from
to repeal part of a law; restrict or modify part of a law
la:verb:derogo.html:
dē-rŏgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a., jurid. t. t.,
to repeal a part of a law, to restrict or modify it.
Prop.: huic legi nec obrogari fas est, neque derogari ex hac aliquid licet, neque tota abrogari potest,; cf.: de lege aliquid derogare aut legem abrogare,; : derogatur legi, cum pars detrahitur,.—
Transf., beyond the legal sphere, to take away, detract from, to diminish, to remove, withdraw.
With de: de magnificentia aut de honestate quiddam,; cf. : de testium fide,—
With ex: si quid ex hac ipsa (aequitate) accusator derogat,.—
With dat. (so most freq.): non mihi tantum derogo, tametsi nihil arrogo, ut, etc.,: fidem alicui,; ; ; Cels. praef.; ; cf. the foll. no. B.; and simply, fidem,: gratiam nomini,, §104: nihil universorum juri, et saep.—
With abstract subjects: quorum virtuti, generi, rebus gestis, fidem et auctoritatem in testimonio cupiditatis suspicio derogavit,; : ubi certam derogat vetustas fidem,.—
To disparage, dishonor: et derogastis adversum me verba vostra (i. e. me verbis),.
